government.name: City of Vancouver
government.howBuilt: This list draws on City of Vancouver election materials and ballot questions, party platforms and mayoral debate coverage in local news, and recent council decisions on the Villages Plan, the supportive housing pause, and the 2026 property tax freeze. We kept issues the City of Vancouver can act on through zoning, its budget, bylaws, streets, and borrowing; provincial matters such as health care and involuntary care are left out except where council has a direct role.

issues.title: Housing supply and neighbourhood zoning
issues.description: How much new housing Vancouver allows, what kinds, and how quickly it changes lower-density neighbourhoods, after council rejected the Villages Plan in July 2026.
issues.whatItAffects: Renters, first-time buyers, families, homeowners, and the look and feel of neighbourhoods.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets zoning and density rules, adopts area plans, and approves rezonings and development permits.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city approach new housing in neighbourhoods?
viewQuestion.poleA: Allow more apartments and low-rise buildings across more neighbourhoods
viewQuestion.poleB: Grow more gradually and keep neighbourhood scale closer to today's

tradeoffs.context: Housing choices often trade how fast new homes get built against how much existing neighbourhoods change.

gains: More homes could be built sooner, easing pressure on rents and prices
Denser areas may support more transit, shops, and local services
costs: Neighbourhoods may see more traffic, shade, and changes in character
Pipes, schools, and parks may need costly upgrades to keep up

gains: Existing neighbourhoods may keep more of their current scale and feel
Growth may be easier to match with infrastructure and services
costs: Fewer new homes could keep rents and prices higher for longer
More people may commute in from elsewhere in the region

issues.title: Public drug use and community safety
issues.description: How the city responds to street disorder, crime, and open-air drug use, including a non-binding plebiscite on banning hard-drug use in public spaces.
issues.whatItAffects: Residents, businesses, visitors, and people living with addiction or mental illness.
issues.whoDecides: Council approves the police budget, funds bylaw enforcement and outreach, and passes public-space bylaws.

viewQuestion.question: Where should the city put more of its safety effort?
viewQuestion.poleA: More police, bylaw enforcement, and limits on public drug use
viewQuestion.poleB: More outreach workers and non-police crisis response teams

tradeoffs.context: Safety budgets are limited, so more spending on enforcement often means less for outreach, and the reverse.

gains: A visible patrol presence may help people feel safer in public spaces
Police could respond faster to calls about crime and disorder
costs: Policing is costly and may not address addiction or mental illness
Enforcement may move problems to other areas rather than solving them

gains: Trained outreach workers may handle mental-health calls with less conflict
Police time could be freed for crimes that need officers
costs: Results may take longer to show up on the street
Some situations may still need a police response

issues.title: Property taxes and city spending
issues.description: How much the city raises in property taxes each year after a 0% increase in 2026, and which services are funded or trimmed.
issues.whatItAffects: Homeowners, renters through their rent, businesses, and everyone who uses city services.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets the annual property tax rate and approves the operating budget.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city handle its budget?
viewQuestion.poleA: Hold tax increases down, even if some services are reduced
viewQuestion.poleB: Raise taxes as needed to maintain or expand city services

tradeoffs.context: A city budget balances what residents pay against the services and upkeep they receive.

gains: Households and businesses would face smaller tax bills
The city may look harder for savings and efficiencies
costs: Some services or programs may be cut or delayed
Maintenance put off now can cost more later

gains: Services, staffing, and upkeep could keep pace with need
The city may have room to start new programs
costs: Tax bills would rise for owners and, indirectly, renters
Higher costs may weigh on small businesses

issues.title: Supportive housing and homelessness
issues.description: Whether the city resumes contributing land or money to new supportive housing, which it paused in 2025, and how it responds to homelessness.
issues.whatItAffects: People who are unhoused or at risk, nearby residents and businesses, and non-profit housing providers.
issues.whoDecides: Council decides whether to contribute city land or funds, approves sites, and partners with BC Housing and health authorities.

viewQuestion.question: What should the city do about new supportive housing?
viewQuestion.poleA: Resume city support so more supportive housing gets built
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep limits and focus on oversight of existing buildings and treatment

tradeoffs.context: Supportive housing decisions weigh getting more people indoors against how well buildings are run and where they go.

gains: More people could move from streets and shelters into housing
The city could draw more senior-government funding for projects
costs: Some neighbours worry about safety near new buildings
Projects may open without enough health and support services

gains: Attention could go to fixing problems in existing buildings
Funding could shift toward treatment and recovery spaces
costs: Fewer new units could leave more people unhoused for longer
Senior-government money may go to other cities

issues.title: City-built and non-market housing
issues.description: How directly the city should create below-market homes, such as co-ops and rentals on city land, versus relying on private builders and faster approvals.
issues.whatItAffects: Middle- and lower-income renters, co-op members, city finances, and builders.
issues.whoDecides: Council decides how city-owned land is used, whether to borrow or partner for housing, and how permits are processed.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city get more affordable homes built?
viewQuestion.poleA: Have the city build or fund co-ops and rentals on public land
viewQuestion.poleB: Speed up approvals so private builders can deliver more homes

tradeoffs.context: The city can act as a builder and landlord itself, or focus on clearing the way for others to build.

gains: Homes could stay affordable over the long term
The city keeps ownership of land and buildings
costs: Borrowing and operating costs fall partly on taxpayers
Fewer total homes may be built per dollar spent

gains: Faster approvals could lower building costs and add supply
Less public money and risk is tied up in housing
costs: New homes may be priced at market rates many cannot afford
The city has less say over who the homes serve

issues.title: Streets, transit, and cycling
issues.description: How the city divides street space among cars, parking, buses, bikes, and pedestrians, including Broadway bike lanes and parking fees.
issues.whatItAffects: Drivers, transit riders, cyclists, pedestrians, and businesses that depend on street access.
issues.whoDecides: Council controls city streets, bike and bus lanes, speed limits on local roads, and parking rules and fees.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city use its street space?
viewQuestion.poleA: Give more space to bike lanes, bus lanes, and walking
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep more space for driving lanes and parking

tradeoffs.context: Street space is fixed, so adding room for one way of travelling usually takes it from another.

gains: Walking, cycling, and transit trips could be safer and faster
Fewer car trips may reduce emissions and noise
costs: Drivers may face slower trips and less parking
Some businesses worry about losing customer access

gains: Driving and deliveries may stay easier and more predictable
Parking stays more available near homes and shops
costs: Cycling and walking routes may remain less connected
Buses may stay stuck in traffic

issues.title: Climate rules and urban trees
issues.description: How strict the city should be on building emissions, natural gas, and protecting the tree canopy as it grows.
issues.whatItAffects: Builders, homeowners, energy costs, air quality, and neighbourhood shade and green space.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets building bylaw energy rules, tree-protection bylaws, and climate targets for city operations.

viewQuestion.question: How far should the city go on climate and trees?
viewQuestion.poleA: Set stronger climate and tree-protection rules for new building
viewQuestion.poleB: Ease climate rules to lower building costs and leave more choice

tradeoffs.context: Climate and tree rules can cut emissions and add shade but may raise the cost and pace of building.

gains: Emissions could fall and neighbourhoods may get more shade and cooling
Buildings may be ready for future energy rules
costs: New homes and renovations may cost more to build
Some sites may fit fewer homes to save trees

gains: Building could be faster and somewhat cheaper
Owners keep more choice over heating and energy
costs: Emissions may fall more slowly
Tree cover may decline as sites redevelop

issues.title: Borrowing for city facilities
issues.description: Whether the city should borrow $790 million, as asked in three ballot questions, to renew streets, bridges, community centres, and parks.
issues.whatItAffects: Users of community centres, pools, parks, roads, and bridges, and future tax bills that repay debt.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets the capital plan, but voters must approve the borrowing questions on the ballot.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city pay to renew aging facilities?
viewQuestion.poleA: Borrow more now to renew and add facilities sooner
viewQuestion.poleB: Borrow less and fund renewal more slowly from current budgets

tradeoffs.context: Borrowing spreads the cost of facilities over the years people use them, but adds interest and debt payments.

gains: Aging facilities could be repaired or replaced sooner
Costs are spread over future users, not just today's taxpayers
costs: Interest and debt payments add to future budgets
Less room may remain for other spending later

gains: The city carries less debt and pays less interest
Future councils keep more budget flexibility
costs: Repairs and new facilities may take longer
Construction costs may rise while projects wait

election.howToVote: Eligible voters can vote at any of 85 voting places on General Voting Day (Saturday, Oct. 17, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.) or at any of 59 advance voting places on Oct. 3, 7, 10 or 13. Voters who are not already registered can register at the voting place with two pieces of ID that together show their name, with an address on at least one and a signature on at least one. Bringing the voter information card mailed in September speeds things up.
election.voteByMail: Mail ballot packages had to be requested by noon Oct. 5 for mailing, or can be picked up at the Election Office (305 West 8th Ave.) until noon Oct. 13; completed ballots must be received by 8 p.m. Oct. 17.

ballotQuestions.question: Are you in favour of Council having the authority, without further assent of the electors, to borrow an aggregate $292,000,000 for transportation and street infrastructure?
ballotQuestions.summary: Asks voters to approve borrowing up to $292 million for bridges and structures, pavement and sidewalks, and traffic signals and street lighting.

ballotQuestions.question: Are you in favour of Council having the authority, without further assent of the electors, to borrow an aggregate $438,000,000 for community serving and civic essential infrastructure?
ballotQuestions.summary: Asks voters to approve borrowing up to $438 million to renew and upgrade community facilities and other civic buildings.

ballotQuestions.question: Are you in favour of Council having the authority, without further assent of the electors, to borrow an aggregate $60,000,000 for parks and open public spaces infrastructure?
ballotQuestions.summary: Asks voters to approve borrowing up to $60 million for renewal, maintenance and upgrades of parks.

ballotQuestions.question: Are you in favour of the City of Vancouver strengthening its laws to forbid open-air hard drug (Heroin, Meth, Fentanyl, and Crack) use in public spaces?
ballotQuestions.summary: A non-binding plebiscite added by council to gauge support for stronger city laws against hard-drug use in public spaces.

ballotQuestions.question: Should the City of Vancouver formally ask the Province of BC to convert portions of the old St. Paul's Hospital, or another similar site, into a secure medical facility that provides acute voluntary and 100-plus involuntary care beds for individuals posing a serious risk to themselves or others due to severe substance use and mental health disorders?
ballotQuestions.summary: A non-binding plebiscite asking whether the city should request that the province create a secure care facility; the decision rests with the province.

electorOrganizations.name: ABC Vancouver
electorOrganizations.blurb: Civic party of incumbent Mayor Ken Sim. Its 2026 platform frames its campaign around keeping Vancouver 'moving forward' with a city that works for residents.

electorOrganizations.name: Bright Future Vancouver
electorOrganizations.blurb: Describes its plan as aimed at renters, trade workers and local families, funded in part by a surcharge on the wealthiest residents.

electorOrganizations.name: COPE
electorOrganizations.blurb: Coalition of Progressive Electors. Says it focuses on housing, climate change and limiting the influence of wealth on politics.

electorOrganizations.name: Green
electorOrganizations.blurb: Green Party of Vancouver, a municipal party with elected representatives on city council, school board and park board.

electorOrganizations.name: OneCity
electorOrganizations.blurb: Founded in 2014 by workers, neighbours and advocates; describes itself as a 'practical progressive' team funded by grassroots donations.

electorOrganizations.name: TEAM
electorOrganizations.blurb: TEAM for a Livable Vancouver. Says it makes core services and infrastructure the top budget priority and favours neighbourhood-based community planning.

electorOrganizations.name: TrueBlue Vancouver
electorOrganizations.blurb: Describes itself as a municipal party advancing practical solutions on housing, public safety, fiscal discipline and downtown recovery.

electorOrganizations.name: Vancouver Liberals
electorOrganizations.blurb: Says it is working for a city that works for everyone, focused on affordability, accountability, public safety, jobs and long-term growth.

electorOrganizations.name: Vote Vancouver
electorOrganizations.blurb: Founded in 2026 by former councillor Rebecca Bligh; describes itself as non-partisan and collaborative, placing itself in the political centre.

electorOrganizations.name: Affordable Housing
electorOrganizations.blurb: Its website identifies it as the Affordable Housing Coalition of Vancouver. It is running one council candidate, Eric Redmond.

candidates.name: Muhammad Ahmad
candidates.summary: Communications and public affairs professional raised in Lahore, Pakistan; chairs a consulting firm's advisory board and is vice-president of a Dunbar preschool board. Father of three living in Vancouver; first run for office.

positions.summary: Bright Future platform: 2,000 rent-to-own homes in a first term, with 20% of rent held in an equity trust owned by the renter.
Bright Future platform: a 2% surcharge on properties worth $5 million or more to fund city initiatives.
positions.leanReason: New tax revenue to fund expanded services

positions.summary: Bright Future platform: free transit for Vancouver residents, safer stations, faster buses, and readiness for SkyTrain to UBC.
Proposes reinstating living wage requirements for City Hall jobs, along with expanded childcare.

candidates.name: Kareem Allam
candidates.summary: Lifelong Vancouverite and partner at Richardson Strategy Group; former public policy director at the Vancouver Board of Trade and Fraser Health board member, with over 25 years in government and policy roles.

positions.summary: At a September debate, supported floor space ratios above 1.25, varying with transit proximity, and SkyTrain to UBC as a priority.
Would reverse the city's pause on new supportive housing on day one, including housing for seniors, veterans and vulnerable residents.
Would replace the Vancouver Building Bylaw with the B.C. Building Code and merge 12 housing-approval departments into one.
Proposes more Vancouver Police funding, added financial-crimes investigators, a methamphetamine strategy, and shutting down Bitcoin ATMs to fight money laundering.
Platform pledges $1.35 billion for parks, pools, rinks and community centres and would cancel a second City Hall project.
Proposes halving property taxes for family doctors' clinics and businesses hit by transit construction, a luxury yacht tax, and removing beach parking fees.
positions.leanReason: Targeted changes, overall level not stated

candidates.name: Rebecca Bligh
candidates.summary: Two-term Vancouver city councillor, first elected in 2018 with the NPA and re-elected in 2022 with ABC, which removed her from its caucus in 2025. Founded a consulting business and launched Vote Vancouver in 2026.

positions.summary: At a September debate, supported a 1.25 floor space ratio and said not proceeding with three to five Villages pilot locations was a failure.
Would build permanently affordable homes for middle-income earners on public land, with not-for-profit childcare included.
positions.leanReason: City builds housing on public land

positions.summary: Supports expanding supportive housing with embedded health services; her March 2026 motion to end the city's pause did not pass.
Supports property tax increases at a sustainable, predictable rate and says a zero-per-cent increase is not sustainable.
positions.leanReason: Accepts steady increases to fund services

positions.summary: Says more police spending alone has not made people feel safer and favours broader approaches addressing underlying causes.
Open to municipal bonds and other financing to renew facilities now and repay the cost over the long term.

candidates.name: Pete Fry
candidates.summary: Two-term Vancouver city councillor, first elected in 2018 and re-elected in 2022; chairs council's Auditor General Committee. Previously a self-employed graphic designer and communications consultant and longtime Strathcona community advocate.

positions.summary: At a September debate, supported higher floor space ratios than 1.25 where tree canopy cover can be preserved.
Pledged at a September debate to reverse the city's pause on city-funded supportive housing.
Green platform: a 24/7 team of non-police community outreach workers for homelessness and mental-health calls, plus an Office of Community Safety.
Green platform: convert at least 11% of road space to walking, cycling and green space, add bus lanes and Broadway bike lanes.
Green platform: adopt a 3-30-300 tree standard, strengthen tree-protection bylaws, and create a municipal arborist office.

candidates.name: Colleen Hardwick
candidates.summary: Former Vancouver city councillor (2018 to 2022) with a background in urban geography and planning. Worked in film production and developed PlaceSpeak, a civic engagement platform. TEAM's mayoral candidate in 2022.

positions.summary: TEAM pledges to repeal up to six plans, including the Broadway, Vancouver and Villages plans, and return to neighbourhood-based community planning.
Says upzoning drives land speculation; wants government and private developers to jointly deliver middle-income and supportive housing.
Would cap property tax increases at inflation and conduct a line-by-line review of the city budget.
TEAM platform: a residents' safety plan targeting repeat offenders, no open drug use in shared public spaces, more enforcement on street disorder.

candidates.name: Ken Sim
candidates.summary: Mayor of Vancouver since 2022, born and raised in the city. A former accountant and investment banker who co-founded home-care company Nurse Next Door and Rosemary Rocksalt bagels; narrowly lost the 2018 mayoral race.

positions.summary: ABC platform: a zero-per-cent property tax increase in 2027, plus ending residential parking permit fees and paid parking at beaches and community centres.
ABC platform: ban hard-drug use in public spaces, simplify police drug seizures, push for 100 involuntary care beds, and keep consumption sites away from schools.

positions.summary: Introduced the 2025 pause on new supportive housing, saying Vancouver has a disproportionate share of such buildings in the region.

ABC platform: $400 million for community centre upgrades, new aquatic centres in Sunset and Marpole, and $104 million for roads and sidewalks.

candidates.name: Amanda Boggan
candidates.summary: Downtown Eastside resident and former president of the Downtown Eastside Neighbourhood Council; has worked in warehouses and laundries and is a long-time civic participant.

positions.summary: Says council should act within its legal authority, with transparency and access to information, and focus on core neighbourhood services.
TEAM pledges to repeal six citywide and area plans, including the Broadway and Villages plans, in favour of neighbourhood-based planning.
TEAM platform: a "predictable property tax" pledge and a line-by-line budget review focused on core services.
TEAM platform: a residents' safety action plan, community-focused policing, and a recovery-focused approach to addiction.

candidates.name: Iona Bonamis

OneCity platform: create community-led crisis teams of social workers for calls not needing police; review police budget like other services.

candidates.summary: Small business owner and Vancouver Pride Society president with over 30 years in small business, community leadership and housing operations.

positions.summary: Prioritizes more affordable, accessible housing options, especially for seniors, so people can stay in their communities.

positions.summary: Wants neighbourhoods built through partnerships and inclusive spaces, welcoming diverse and LGBTQ2S+ residents and reducing isolation.
